candidate_relations.reason: Neuralgic amyotrophy and Parsonage-Turner Syndrome are the same diagnostic entity. The clinical picture (young woman, sudden focal upper limb weakness, EMG showing neurogenic changes beyond a single nerve territory including biceps, triceps, and deltoid in addition to AIN-innervated muscles, no sensory deficit, normal MRI) is consistent with this diagnosis. The term is a complete alias.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Neuralgic amyotrophy is the established synonym for Parsonage-Turner Syndrome

candidate_relations.reason: Although the patient's motor deficits (thumb distal phalanx, index finger, inability to form OK sign) suggest AIN involvement, the EMG also shows neurogenic changes in biceps, triceps, and deltoid — muscles outside the AIN territory. This multi-nerve/plexus involvement is the hallmark of Parsonage-Turner Syndrome, not isolated AIN syndrome. Labeling it AIN Syndrome would assert an incompatible, narrower anatomical scope.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Anterior Interosseous Nerve Syndrome is a mononeuropathy confined to the AIN territory, whereas the reference diagnosis is a broader brachial plexopathy/neuritis

candidate_relations.reason: This label is functionally equivalent to C002 (isolated AIN neuropathy). The EMG evidence of involvement of biceps, triceps, and deltoid muscles extends well beyond the AIN distribution, making a diagnosis limited to the anterior interosseous nerve anatomically incompatible with the full clinical picture consistent with Parsonage-Turner Syndrome.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Same reasoning as C002 — neuropathy of the anterior interosseous nerve is anatomically restricted and does not account for the broader EMG findings

case_quality_flags: EMG findings extending beyond AIN territory (biceps, triceps, deltoid) are the critical discriminator between isolated AIN syndrome and Parsonage-Turner Syndrome
